I feel strained, half stranded, as ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But ere I break, ye’ll hear me crack; and till ye hear that, know that Ahab’s hawser tows his purpose yet. Believe ye, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For ere they drown, drowning things will twice rise to the surface; then rise again, to sink for evermore. So with Moby Dick—two days he’s floated—tomorrow will be the third. Aye, men, he’ll rise once more,—but only to spout his last! D’ye feel brave men, brave?”
“As fearless fire,” cried Stubb.

“And as mechanical,” muttered Ahab. Then as the men went forward, he muttered on: “The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same to Starbuck there, concerning my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I seek to drive out of others’ hearts what’s clinched so fast in mine!—The Parsee—the Parsee!—gone, gone? and he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How’s that?—There’s a riddle now might baffle all the lawyers backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges:—like a hawk’s beak it pecks my brain. I’ll, I’ll solve it, though!”
When dusk descended, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

So once more the sail was shortened, and everything passed nearly as on the previous night; only, the sound of hammers, and the hum of the grindstone was heard till nearly daylight, as the men toiled by lanterns in the complete and careful rigging of the spare boats and sharpening their fresh weapons for the morrow. Meantime, of the broken keel of Ahab’s wrecked craft the carpenter made him another leg; while still as on the night before, slouched Ahab stood fixed within his scuttle; his hid, heliotrope glance anticipatingly gone backward on its dial; sat due eastward for the earliest sun.

“Aye, aye, Starbuck, ’tis sweet to lean sometimes, be the leaner who he will; and would old Ahab had leaned oftener than he has.”
“The ferrule has not stood, sir,” said the carpenter, now coming up; “I put good work into that leg.”
“But no bones broken, sir, I hope,” said Stubb with true concern.

“Aye! and all splintered to pieces, Stubb!—d’ye see it.—But even with a broken bone, old Ahab is untouched; and I account no living bone of mine one jot more me, than this dead one that’s lost. Nor white whale, nor man, nor fiend, can so much as graze old Ahab in his own proper and inaccessible being. Can any lead touch yonder floor, any mast scrape yonder roof?—Aloft there! which way?”
“Dead to leeward, sir.”
“Up helm, then; pile on the sail again, ship keepers! down the rest of the spare boats and rig them—Mr. Starbuck away, and muster the boat’s crews.”
“Let me first help thee towards the bulwarks, sir.”
“Oh, oh, oh! how this splinter gores me now! Accursed fate! that the unconquerable captain in the soul should have such a craven mate!”
“Sir?”
“My body, man, not thee. Give me something for a cane—there, that shivered lance will do. Muster the men. Surely I have not seen him yet. By heaven it cannot be!—missing?—quick! call them all.”
The old man’s hinted thought was true. Upon mustering the company, the Parsee was not there.
“The Parsee!” cried Stubb—“he must have been caught in——”
“The black vomit wrench thee!—run all of ye above, alow, cabin, forecastle—find him—not gone—not gone!”
But quickly they returned to him with the tidings that the Parsee was nowhere to be found.
“Aye, sir,” said Stubb—“caught among the tangles of your line—I thought I saw him dragging under.”

“_My_ line! _my_ line? Gone?—gone? What means that little word?—What death-knell rings in it, that old Ahab shakes as if he were the belfry. The harpoon, too!—toss over the litter there,—d’ye see it?—the forged iron, men, the white whale’s—no, no, no,—blistered fool! this hand did dart it!—’tis in the fish!—Aloft there! Keep him nailed—Quick!—all hands to the rigging of the boats—collect the oars—harpooneers! the irons, the irons!—hoist the royals higher—a pull on all the sheets!—helm there! steady, steady for your life! I’ll ten times girdle the unmeasured globe; yea and dive straight through it, but I’ll slay him yet!”

“Great God! but for one single instant show thyself,” cried Starbuck; “never, never wilt thou capture him, old man—In Jesus’ name no more of this, that’s worse than devil’s madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; thy very leg once more snatched from under thee; thy evil shadow gone—all good angels mobbing thee with warnings:—what more wouldst thou have?—Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh,—Impiety and blasphemy to hunt him more!”

“Starbuck, of late I’ve felt strangely moved to thee; ever since that hour we both saw—thou know’st what, in one another’s eyes. But in this matter of the whale, be the front of thy face to me as the palm of this hand—a lipless, unfeatured blank. Ahab is for ever Ahab, man. This whole act’s immutably decreed. ’Twas rehearsed by thee and me a billion years before this ocean rolled. Fool! I am the Fates’ lieutenant; I act under orders. Look thou, underling! that thou obeyest mine.—Stand round me, men. Ye see an old man cut down to the stump; leaning on a shivered lance; propped up on a lonely foot. ’Tis Ahab—his body’s part; but Ahab’s soul’s a centipede, that moves upon a hundred legs. I feel strained, half stranded, as ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But ere I break, ye’ll hear me crack; and till ye hear _that_, know that Ahab’s hawser tows his purpose yet. Believe ye, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For ere they drown, drowning things will twice rise to the surface; then rise again, to sink for evermore. So with Moby Dick—two days he’s floated—tomorrow will be the third. Aye, men, he’ll rise once more,—but only to spout his last! D’ye feel brave men, brave?”
“As fearless fire,” cried Stubb.

“And as mechanical,” muttered Ahab. Then as the men went forward, he muttered on: “The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same to Starbuck there, concerning my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I seek to drive out of others’ hearts what’s clinched so fast in mine!—The Parsee—the Parsee!—gone, gone? and he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How’s that?—There’s a riddle now might baffle all the lawyers backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges:—like a hawk’s beak it pecks my brain. _I’ll_, _I’ll_ solve it, though!”
When dusk descended, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

So once more the sail was shortened, and everything passed nearly as on the previous night; only, the sound of hammers, and the hum of the grindstone was heard till nearly daylight, as the men toiled by lanterns in the complete and careful rigging of the spare boats and sharpening their fresh weapons for the morrow. Meantime, of the broken keel of Ahab’s wrecked craft the carpenter made him another leg; while still as on the night before, slouched Ahab stood fixed within his scuttle; his hid, heliotrope glance anticipatingly gone backward on its dial; sat due eastward for the earliest sun.

modern_en.title: Chapter 134 — The Chase—Second Day
paragraphs: At daybreak, the three mastheads were promptly manned again.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab, after allowing a little time for the light to spread.
"See nothing, sir."
"Turn up all hands and make sail! He travels faster than I thought — the topgallant sails! — aye, they should have been kept on her all night. But no matter — he's only resting for the rush."

Let it be said here that this persistent pursuit of one particular whale, kept up through day into night and through night into day, is by no means unheard of in the South Sea fishery. For such is the wonderful skill, the foresight born of experience, and the unshakable confidence acquired by some great natural geniuses among the Nantucket captains, that from simply observing a whale when last sighted they will, under certain given circumstances, predict pretty accurately both the direction in which he will keep swimming for a while out of sight, and his probable rate of progress during that time. In these cases the whale-fisherman does somewhat as a pilot does when he is about to lose sight of a coast whose general trend he knows well, and which he wants to return to shortly, but at some further point: just as this pilot stands by his compass and takes the exact bearing of the cape now in view, so as to be surer of hitting the remote, unseen headland he will eventually reach, so the fisherman stands at his compass with the whale; for after the creature has been chased and carefully marked through several hours of daylight, then, when night hides the fish, its future wake through the darkness is almost as settled in the hunter's shrewd mind as the pilot's coast is in his. So, to this hunter's wondrous skill, a wake — that proverbially fleeting thing written in water — is for all desired purposes nearly as reliable as the steadfast land. And just as the mighty iron Leviathan of the modern railway is so familiarly known in its every pace that men, watches in hand, time his rate as doctors time a baby's pulse, and say casually that the up train or the down train will reach such and such a spot at such and such an hour, so, almost, there are occasions when these Nantucketers time that other Leviathan of the deep by the observed humor of his speed, and say to themselves that so many hours from now this whale will have gone two hundred miles, and will have about reached this or that degree of latitude or longitude. But for this sharpness to succeed at all in the end, the wind and the sea must be the whaleman's allies; for what use at the moment to the becalmed or windbound sailor is the skill that assures him he is exactly ninety-three leagues and a quarter from his port? Many further subtle points concerning the chase of whales can be inferred from these statements.
The ship tore on, leaving a furrow in the sea like the one a stray cannonball makes when it turns plowshare and furrows up the level field.

"By salt and hemp!" cried Stubb, "but this swift motion of the deck creeps up one's legs and tingles at the heart. This ship and I are two brave fellows! — Ha, ha! Someone pick me up and launch me spine-first on the sea — for, by live-oaks! my spine's a keel. Ha, ha! We go the gait that leaves no dust behind!"
"There she blows — she blows! — she blows! — right ahead!" was now the cry from the masthead.

"Aye, aye!" cried Stubb. "I knew it — you can't escape — blow on and split your spout, O whale! The mad fiend himself is after you! Blow your trumpet — blister your lungs! — Ahab will dam off your blood, as a miller shuts his watergate on the stream!"

And Stubb was only speaking for nearly the whole crew. The frenzies of the chase had by now worked them up into a bubbling ferment, like old wine fermenting anew. Whatever pale fears and forebodings some of them might have felt before, these were now not only kept out of sight by their growing awe of Ahab, but broken up and routed on all sides, like timid prairie hares scattering before the bounding bison. The hand of Fate had snatched all their souls; and by the stirring dangers of the day before, the torment of the past night's suspense, and the fixed, unfearing, blind, reckless way their wild ship went plunging toward its flying target — by all these things their hearts were bowled along. The wind that swelled their sails into great bellies and rushed the vessel on with arms as invisible as they were irresistible seemed the symbol of that unseen power which so enslaved them to the race.

They were one man, not thirty. For just as the one ship that held them all, though it was put together from all sorts of contrasting things — oak, and maple, and pine; iron, and pitch, and hemp — yet had all these running into one another in the single solid hull, which shot on its way both balanced and steered by the long central keel, so all the individualities of the crew — this man's courage, that man's fear, guilt and guiltiness — all these varieties were welded into oneness, and all were directed toward that fatal goal which Ahab, their one lord and keel, pointed to.

The rigging was alive. The mastheads, like the tops of tall palms, sprouted outspreading tufts of arms and legs. Clinging to a spar with one hand, some reached out the other with impatient waves; others, shading their eyes from the vivid sunlight, sat far out on the rocking yards; every spar bore its full crop of mortals, ready and ripe for their fate. Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!

"Why don't you sing out for him, if you see him?" cried Ahab, when some minutes had passed since the first cry and no more had been heard. "Sway me up, men; you have been deceived. Moby Dick does not cast one odd jet that way and then disappear."

It was just so; in their headlong eagerness the men had mistaken something else for the whale's spout, as the event itself soon proved; for hardly had Ahab reached his perch, hardly was the rope made fast to its pin on deck, when he struck the keynote for an orchestra that made the air vibrate as if with the combined discharge of rifles. The triumphant shout of thirty buckskin lungs was heard as — much nearer the ship than the place of the imaginary jet, less than a mile ahead — Moby Dick burst bodily into view! For the White Whale now revealed his nearness not by any calm and lazy spouting, not by the peaceful gush of that mystic fountain in his head, but by the far more wondrous phenomenon of breaching. Rising at his utmost speed from the farthest depths, the Sperm Whale in this way booms his entire bulk into the pure element of air, and, piling up a mountain of dazzling foam, shows where he is to a distance of seven miles and more. At such moments the torn, enraged waves he shakes off seem to be his mane; in some cases this breaching is his act of defiance.

"There she breaches! There she breaches!" was the cry, as in his immeasurable bravado the White Whale tossed himself salmon-like to Heaven. Seen so suddenly in the blue plain of the sea, and set off against the still bluer edge of the sky, the spray he raised glittered and glared unbearably for the moment, like a glacier; and it stood there, gradually fading and fading from its first sparkling intensity to the dim mistiness of a shower advancing up a valley.
"Aye, breach your last to the sun, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Your hour and your harpoon are at hand! — Down! Down, all of you, but one man at the fore. The boats! — stand by!"

Ignoring the tedious rope-ladders of the shrouds, the men slid to the deck like shooting stars by the lone backstays and halyards, while Ahab, less dartingly but still rapidly, was lowered from his perch.
"Lower away," he cried, as soon as he had reached his boat — a spare one, rigged the afternoon before. "Mr. Starbuck, the ship is yours — keep away from the boats, but keep near them. Lower, all!"

As if to strike quick terror into them — being by this time the first to attack — Moby Dick had turned and was now coming for the three crews. Ahab's boat was in the center; and cheering his men on, he told them he would take the whale head-and-head — that is, pull straight up to his forehead — which is not an uncommon thing; for within a certain distance such a course keeps the coming attack out of the whale's sideways vision. But before that close range was reached, and while all three boats were still as plain to his eye as the ship's three masts, the White Whale, churning himself into a furious speed, rushed among the boats almost in an instant, as it were, with open jaws and lashing tail, and offered appalling battle on every side; and heedless of the irons darted at him from every boat, he seemed intent only on annihilating each separate plank those boats were made of. But skillfully maneuvered, wheeling ceaselessly like trained war-horses on the field, the boats evaded him for a while, though at times only by a plank's breadth; while all the time Ahab's unearthly war cry tore every other cry but his to shreds.

But at last, in his untraceable twists and turns, the White Whale so crossed and recrossed, and in a thousand ways so tangled the slack of the three lines now fast to him, that they shortened and, of themselves, hauled the doomed boats toward the irons planted in him; though now for a moment the whale drew a little aside, as if to rally for a more tremendous charge. Seizing that chance, Ahab first paid out more line, and then began rapidly hauling and jerking it in again — hoping that way to clear it of some snarls — when look! — a sight more savage than the embattled teeth of sharks!

Caught and twisted — corkscrewed in the tangles of the line — loose harpoons and lances, with all their bristling barbs and points, came flashing and dripping up to the chocks in the bow of Ahab's boat. Only one thing could be done. Seizing the boat-knife, he reached with precise care within — through — and then out beyond — the rays of steel; dragged in the line beyond them, passed it inboard to the bowsman, and then, cutting the rope twice near the chocks, dropped the intercepted bundle of steel into the sea, and was all fast again. At that instant the White Whale made a sudden rush among the remaining tangles of the other lines; by doing so he irresistibly dragged the more entangled boats of Stubb and Flask toward his flukes, dashed them together like two husks rolling on a surf-beaten beach, and then, diving down into the sea, disappeared in a boiling maelstrom, in which, for a while, the fragrant cedar chips of the wrecks danced round and round like grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch.

While the two crews were still circling in the water, reaching out after the revolving line-tubs, oars, and other floating gear; while little Flask, slanting, bobbed up and down like an empty vial, twitching his legs upward to escape the dreaded jaws of sharks; and Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to ladle him up; and while the old man's line — now parting — allowed him to pull into the creamy pool to rescue whom he could — in that wild simultaneous rush of a thousand massed perils, Ahab's still unstruck boat seemed drawn up toward Heaven by invisible wires, as, arrow-like, shooting straight up out of the sea, the White Whale dashed his broad forehead against its bottom and sent it turning over and over into the air, until it fell again, gunwale downward, and Ahab and his men struggled out from under it like seals from a seaside cave.

The whale's first upward momentum — changing its direction as he struck the surface — carried him along it, without his willing it, to a little distance from the center of the destruction he had made; and with his back to it he now lay for a moment, slowly feeling from side to side with his flukes; and whenever a stray oar, a bit of plank, or the least chip or crumb of the boats touched his skin, his tail swiftly drew back and came sideways, smiting the sea. But soon, as if satisfied that his work for that time was done, he pushed his pleated forehead through the ocean and, trailing the intertangled lines after him, continued on his way to leeward at a traveler's steady pace.

As before, the watchful ship had seen the whole fight and again came bearing down to the rescue; lowering a boat, she picked up the floating sailors, tubs, oars, and whatever else could be caught hold of, and landed them safely on her decks. Some sprained shoulders, wrists, and ankles; livid bruises; wrenched harpoons and lances; hopeless tangles of rope; shattered oars and planks — all these were there; but no fatal or even serious harm seemed to have come to anyone. As with Fedallah the day before, Ahab was now found grimly clinging to his boat's broken half, which made a comparatively easy float; nor did this mishap exhaust him as much as the previous day's had.

But when he was helped onto the deck, all eyes were fixed on him; for instead of standing by himself he still hung half his weight on the shoulder of Starbuck, who had so far been the first to help him. His ivory leg had been snapped off, leaving only one short, sharp splinter.
"Aye, aye, Starbuck, it's sweet to lean sometimes, whoever the leaner may be; and I wish old Ahab had leaned more often than he has."
"The ferrule has not held, sir," said the carpenter, now coming up; "I put good work into that leg."
"But no bones broken, sir, I hope," said Stubb with true concern.

"Aye! And all splintered to pieces, Stubb! — do you see it? — But even with a broken bone, old Ahab is untouched; and I count no living bone of mine one jot more me than this dead one that's lost. Neither white whale, nor man, nor fiend can so much as graze old Ahab in his own proper and inaccessible being. Can any lead touch that floor down there, any mast scrape that roof up there? — Aloft there! Which way?"
"Dead to leeward, sir."
"Up helm, then; pile on the sail again, shipkeepers! Down with the rest of the spare boats and rig them — Mr. Starbuck, away, and muster the boats' crews."
"Let me first help you toward the bulwarks, sir."
"Oh, oh, oh! How this splinter gores me now! Cursed fate! That the unconquerable captain in the soul should have such a cowardly mate!"
"Sir?"

"My body, man, not you. Give me something for a cane — there, that shattered lance will do. Muster the men. Surely I have not seen him yet. By heaven, it cannot be! — missing? — quick! Call them all."
The old man's half-spoken thought was true. When the company was mustered, the Parsee was not there.
"The Parsee!" cried Stubb — "he must have been caught in — "
"May the black vomit wrench you! — run, all of you, above, below, cabin, forecastle — find him — not gone — not gone!"
But they quickly came back to him with the news that the Parsee was nowhere to be found.
"Aye, sir," said Stubb — "caught among the tangles of your line — I thought I saw him dragging under."

"My line! My line? Gone? — gone? What does that little word mean? — What death-knell rings in it, that old Ahab shakes as if he were the belfry? The harpoon, too! — toss over the litter there — do you see it? — the forged iron, men, the white whale's — no, no, no — blistered fool! this hand did dart it! — it's in the fish! — Aloft there! Keep him nailed — quick! — all hands to the rigging of the boats — collect the oars — harpooners! the irons, the irons! — hoist the royals higher — a pull on all the sheets! — helm there! Steady, steady for your life! I'll girdle the unmeasured globe ten times; yes, and dive straight through it, but I'll slay him yet!"

"Great God! Show yourself, if only for one single instant," cried Starbuck; "never, never will you capture him, old man — in Jesus' name, no more of this; it's worse than devil's madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; your very leg snatched from under you once more; your evil shadow gone — all good angels mobbing you with warnings — what more do you want? — Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh — it is impiety and blasphemy to hunt him any more!"

"Starbuck, lately I've felt strangely moved toward you, ever since that hour when we both saw — you know what — in one another's eyes. But in this matter of the whale, let the front of your face be to me as the palm of this hand — a lipless, featureless blank. Ahab is forever Ahab, man. This whole act is immutably decreed. You and I rehearsed it a billion years before this ocean rolled. Fool! I am the Fates' lieutenant; I act under orders. See to it, underling, that you obey mine. — Stand round me, men. You see an old man cut down to the stump, leaning on a shattered lance, propped up on a lonely foot. That is Ahab — his body's part; but Ahab's soul's a centipede that moves on a hundred legs. I feel strained, half stranded, like ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But before I break, you'll hear me crack; and till you hear that — know that Ahab's hawser tows his purpose yet. Do you believe, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For before they drown, drowning things will rise twice to the surface; then rise again, to sink forevermore. So with Moby Dick — two days he's floated — tomorrow will be the third. Aye, men, he'll rise once more — but only to spout his last! Do you feel brave, men, brave?"
"As fearless fire," cried Stubb.

"And as mechanical," muttered Ahab. Then, as the men went forward, he muttered on: "The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same way to Starbuck there, about my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I try to drive out of others' hearts what's clinched so fast in mine! — The Parsee — the Parsee! — gone, gone? And he was to go before — but still was to be seen again before I could perish — how's that? — There's a riddle now that might baffle all the lawyers, backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges — it pecks my brain like a hawk's beak. I — I will solve it, though!"
When dusk came down, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

So once more the sail was shortened, and everything passed nearly as on the night before; except that the sound of hammers and the hum of the grindstone were heard until nearly daylight, as the men toiled by lantern light at the complete and careful rigging of the spare boats and the sharpening of their fresh weapons for the next day. Meanwhile, out of the broken keel of Ahab's wrecked boat the carpenter made him another leg; while, still as on the night before, Ahab stood slouched and fixed within his scuttle, his hidden, heliotrope glance — sun-seeking, like the flower — turned back ahead of time on its dial, set due east for the earliest sun.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 134 — Jagten — Anden dag
paragraphs: Ved daggry var de tre mastetoppe straks besat igen.
»Ser I ham?« råbte Ahab, efter at have ventet lidt, så lyset kunne brede sig.
»Ser ingenting, sir.«
»Alle mand op og sæt sejl! Han svømmer hurtigere, end jeg troede. — Bramsejlene! — Ja, dem skulle vi have haft på hende hele natten. Men lige meget. Han hviler bare, før han styrter af sted.«

Det skal siges her, at denne udholdende jagt på én bestemt hval, ført videre gennem dag og ind i nat og gennem nat og ind i dag, på ingen måde er uhørt i sydhavsfangsten. For nogle af de store naturgenier blandt Nantucket-kaptajnerne har en så forunderlig kunnen, en så erfaringsfødt forudseenhed og en så urokkelig tillid, at de blot ved at se på en hval, når den sidst blev set, under visse givne omstændigheder kan forudsige temmelig nøjagtigt både den retning, han vil blive ved med at svømme i et stykke tid uden for synsvidde, og den fart, han sandsynligvis har i mellemtiden. I disse tilfælde gør hvalfangeren noget i retning af det, en lods gør, når han er ved at miste en kyst af syne, hvis almindelige forløb han kender godt, og som han snart vil vende tilbage til, men ved et andet punkt længere fremme. Ligesom lodsen står ved sit kompas og tager den nøjagtige pejling af det forbjerg, han nu ser, for at være desto sikrere på at ramme det fjerne, usete forbjerg, han til sidst når frem til, således står fiskeren ved sit kompas med hvalen. For når dyret er blevet jagtet og omhyggeligt fulgt gennem flere timer af dagen, og natten så skjuler fisken, er dens kommende kølvand gennem mørket næsten lige så fast i jægerens skarpe sind, som lodsens kyst er i hans. Så for denne jægers vidunderlige kunnen er et kølvand, den ordsprogligt flygtige ting, skrevet i vand, til alle ønskede formål næsten lige så pålideligt som det faste land. Og ligesom den mægtige jernleviatan, jernbanen i vore dage, er så velkendt i hvert eneste skridt, at folk med ur i hånden tager tid på dens fart, som læger tæller en babys puls, og henkastet siger, at toget op eller toget ned når et bestemt sted på et bestemt tidspunkt, således gør nantucketerne næsten det samme ved den anden leviatan i dybet. De tager tid på ham efter hans iagttagne fartlune og siger til sig selv, at om så og så mange timer vil denne hval have svømmet to hundrede engelske mil og omtrent have nået den og den bredde- eller længdegrad. Men for at denne skarpsindighed overhovedet kan lykkes til sidst, må vind og hav være hvalfangerens forbundsfæller. For hvad nytte har den dygtighed i øjeblikket for den sejler, der ligger i stille eller er fanget af modvind, når den fortæller ham, at han ligger præcis treoghalvfems mil og en fjerdedel fra sin havn? Mange andre fine pointer om jagten på hvaler kan udledes af disse udsagn.
Skibet fór af sted og efterlod en fure i havet, som den en forvildet kanonkugle laver, når den bliver til plovjern og pløjer den jævne mark op.

»Ved salt og hamp!« råbte Stubb. »Men den hurtige bevægelse i dækket kryber op ad benene og kilder helt ind i hjertet. Dette skib og jeg er to tapre knægte! — Ha, ha! Nogen skal samle mig op og sende mig ud på havet med rygraden først — for ved levende egetræ! min rygrad er en køl. Ha, ha! Vi går i den fart, der ikke efterlader noget støv!«
»Der blæser hun — hun blæser! — hun blæser! — lige forude!« lød nu råbet fra mastetoppen.

»Ja, ja!« råbte Stubb. »Jeg vidste det. Du kan ikke slippe væk. Bliv ved med at blæse og flæng din blæsning, o hval! Selve den gale djævel er efter dig! Blæs i din trompet — brænd dine lunger til blærer! — Ahab vil dæmme op for dit blod, som en møller lukker sit sluseværk for åen!«

Og Stubb talte kun på vegne af næsten hele besætningen. Jagtens vildskab havde nu bragt dem op i en boblende gæring, som gammel vin, der gærer påny. Hvilke blege frygtsomme anelser nogle af dem end havde haft før, var de nu ikke blot holdt skjult af deres voksende ærefrygt for Ahab, men splittet og jaget på flugt til alle sider, som frygtsomme præriehare, der spredes foran den springende bison. Skæbnens hånd havde grebet alle deres sjæle. Dagen før med dens ophidsende farer, den forgangne nats pinsel af uvished og den faste, ufrygtsomme, blinde, hensynsløse måde, hvorpå deres vilde skib styrtede af sted mod sit flygtende mål — alt dette rullede deres hjerter af sted. Vinden, der fyldte deres sejl til store maver og drev skibet fremad med arme så usynlige, som de var uimodståelige, syntes at være et sindbillede på den usete magt, der slavebandt dem så til jagten.

De var ét menneske, ikke tredive. For ligesom det ene skib, der rummede dem alle, selv om det var sat sammen af alle slags modsatrettede ting — eg og ahorn og fyr, jern og beg og hamp — dog lod alt dette løbe ind i hinanden i det ene faste skrog, som fór af sted både holdt på ret køl og styret af den lange midterkøl, således blev alle besætningens særpræg — denne mands mod, hin mands frygt, skyld og uskyld — alle disse forskelligheder svejset sammen til enhed, og alle blev rettet mod det skæbnesvangre mål, som Ahab, deres ene herre og køl, pegede på.

Rigningen var levende. Mastetoppene, som toppene af høje palmer, skød spredte totter af arme og ben ud. Nogle klamrede sig til en rundholt med den ene hånd og rakte den anden ud i utålmodige vink. Andre satte sig langt ude på de gyngende rår og skyggede for øjnene mod det skarpe sollys. Hver eneste rundholt bar sin fulde afgrøde af dødelige, parate og modne til deres skæbne. Ak! hvor de stadig anstrengte sig for at finde det, der kunne ødelægge dem, gennem al den uendelige blå!

»Hvorfor råber I ikke op, hvis I ser ham?« råbte Ahab, da der var gået nogle minutter siden det første råb, og der ikke var hørt flere. »Hejs mig op, mænd. I er blevet narret. Moby Dick sender ikke én enkelt mærkelig stråle den vej og forsvinder så.«

Sådan var det netop. I deres hovedkulds iver havde mændene taget noget andet for hvalens blæst, som begivenheden selv snart viste. For næppe var Ahab nået op til sit sæde, næppe var tovet gjort fast til sin pløk på dækket, før han slog tonen an for et orkester, der fik luften til at dirre, som var det en samlet salve af geværer. Det triumferende råb fra tredive bukkeskindslunger lød, da Moby Dick — meget nærmere skibet end stedet for den indbildte stråle, mindre end en engelsk mil forude — brød frem i fuld legemsstørrelse! For nu afslørede den hvide hval sin nærhed ikke ved nogen rolig og dovnende blæsning, ikke ved den fredelige strøm fra den mystiske fontæne i hans hoved, men ved det langt mere forunderlige fænomen, at springe. Den kaskelot, der stiger op fra de fjerneste dyb i sin højeste fart, kaster på den måde hele sin masse op i den rene luft og viser, mens han tårner et bjerg af blændende skum op, hvor han er, på en afstand af syv engelske mil og mere. I sådanne øjeblikke synes de sønderrevne, ophidsede bølger, han ryster af sig, at være hans manke. I nogle tilfælde er dette spring hans trodsige handling.

»Der springer hun! Der springer hun!« lød råbet, mens den hvide hval i sin umådelige bravade kastede sig som en laks mod himlen. Set så pludseligt på havets blå slette og sat af mod himlens endnu blåere rand glimtede og blændede den sprøjt, han rejste, uudholdeligt et øjeblik som en gletsjer. Og den stod der og blegnede og blegnede fra sin første funklende styrke til den svage dis af en byge, der rykker op gennem en dal.
»Ja, spring din sidste gang mod solen, Moby Dick!« råbte Ahab. »Din time og din harpun er nær! — Ned! Ned, alle sammen, undtagen én mand i fokkemasten. Bådene! — Gør klar!«

Mændene brød sig ikke om de langsomme rebstiger i vanterne, men gled ned på dækket som faldende stjerner ad de enkelte bagstag og faldrebene, mens Ahab, mindre farende, men dog hurtigt, blev firet ned fra sit sæde.

»Fir ned,« råbte han, så snart han var nået til sin båd, en reservebåd, der var gjort klar eftermiddagen før. »Mr. Starbuck, skibet er Deres. Hold Dem væk fra bådene, men hold Dem tæt på dem. Fir ned, alle!«

Som for at slå dem med hurtig skræk, nu hvor han selv var den første til at angribe, havde Moby Dick vendt sig og kom nu efter de tre besætninger. Ahabs båd lå i midten. Og mens han opmuntrede sine mænd, sagde han til dem, at han ville tage hvalen hoved mod hoved, det vil sige ro lige op til hans pande, hvilket ikke er noget ualmindeligt. For inden for en vis afstand holder et sådant kurs det kommende angreb uden for hvalens sidesyn. Men før denne nærhed var nået, og mens alle tre både stadig var lige så tydelige for hans øje som skibets tre master, kastede den hvide hval sig ud i en rasende fart og fór næsten på et øjeblik ind blandt bådene med åbne kæber og piskende hale og bød skrækindjagende kamp til alle sider. Uden at bryde sig om de jern, der blev slynget mod ham fra hver båd, syntes han kun at ville tilintetgøre hver enkelt planke, bådene var bygget af. Men dygtigt manøvrerede, ustandseligt svingende som veltrænede krigsheste på marken undgik bådene ham et stykke tid, til tider dog kun med en plankebredde. Hele tiden rev Ahabs overjordiske krigsråb ethvert andet råb end hans eget i laser.

Men til sidst krydsede og genkrydsede den hvide hval i sine usporlige sving og vendinger og filtrede på tusind måder slækken af de tre liner, der nu sad fast i ham, så meget sammen, at de blev kortere og af sig selv hev de dømte både hen mod de jern, der sad i ham. Dog trak hvalen sig nu et øjeblik lidt til side, som for at samle kræfter til et endnu voldsommere udfald. Ahab greb chancen. Først firede han mere line ud og begyndte så hurtigt at hale og rykke den ind igen i håb om på den måde at få nogle af knuderne fri. Da se! Et syn mere vildt end hajernes kampberedte tænder!

Fanget og snoet — korkskruet ind i linens filtrede sammenfiltring — kom løse harpuner og lanser med alle deres strittende modhager og spidser blinkende og dryppende op til rendeblokkene i stævnen på Ahabs båd. Der var kun én ting at gøre. Ahab greb bådkniven og rakte med præcis omhu ind i — gennem — og ud over — stålstrålerne, trak linen ind bag dem og rakte den indenbords til bovmanden. Så huggede han rebet over to gange nær rendeblokkene, lod det fastklemte bundt stål falde i havet, og alt var fast igen. I samme øjeblik for den hvide hval pludselig ind mellem de sidste filtrede rester af de andre liner. Dermed slæbte han uimodståeligt Stubbs og Flasks mere indfiltrede både hen mod sine halefinner. Han smækkede dem sammen som to skaller, der rulles rundt på en brændingspisket strand, dykkede så ned i havet og forsvandt i en sydende malstrøm. Dér dansede de duftende cedertræsflis fra vragene en tid rundt og rundt som revet muskatnød i en hurtigt omrørt punchebolle.

Mens de to besætninger stadig kredsede i vandet og rakte efter de roterende linetønder, årer og andet flydende grej; mens lille Flask lå skråt og dukkede op og ned som et tomt medicinglas og sprællede med benene opad for at slippe væk fra hajernes frygtede kæber; mens Stubb lystigt råbte efter nogen, der kunne øse ham op; og mens den gamle mands line — nu sprang den — lod ham ro ind i den flødeagtige pøl for at redde, hvem han kunne — i dette vilde, samtidige udbrud af tusind sammenpressede farer virkede det, som om Ahabs endnu uberørte båd blev trukket op mod himlen af usynlige tråde, for den hvide hval skød pilsnart lodret op af havet, stødte sin brede pande mod bådens bund og sendte den snurrende rundt og rundt op i luften, til den faldt ned igen med rælingen nedad. Ahab og hans folk kæmpede sig ud under den som sæler fra en havgrotte.

Hvalens første opadgående fart — som skiftede retning, da han ramte overfladen — bar ham uden hans vilje et lille stykke væk fra midten af den ødelæggelse, han havde skabt. Med ryggen til den lå han nu et øjeblik og famlede langsomt fra side til side med halefinnerne. Og hver gang en vildfaren åre, et stykke planke eller den mindste flis eller krumme af bådene rørte hans hud, trak halen sig hurtigt tilbage og kom sidelæns og slog mod havet. Men snart skubbede han, som om han var tilfreds med, at hans værk for denne gang var gjort, sin rynkede pande gennem havet, og med de sammenfiltrede liner slæbende efter sig fortsatte han ned mod læ i en rejsendes jævne tempo.

Som før havde det årvågne skib set hele kampen og kom igen sejlende ned for at hjælpe. Hun satte en båd i vandet, tog de flydende sømænd, tønder, årer og alt andet, der kunne fanges, om bord og landede dem sikkert på sine dæk. Nogle forstuvede skuldre, håndled og ankler, blå mærker, forvredne harpuner og lanser, håbløse filtrede reb, knuste årer og planker — alt dette var der. Men ingen syntes at have taget dødelig eller bare alvorlig skade. Ligesom Fedallah dagen før blev Ahab nu fundet fast klamrende sig til den ødelagte båds ene halvdel, som gav en forholdsvis let flåde. Og denne ulykke udmattede ham ikke så meget som den foregående dags.

Men da han blev hjulpet op på dækket, hvilede alles øjne på ham. For i stedet for at stå selv lod han stadig halvdelen af sin vægt hvile på skulderen af Starbuck, som indtil nu havde været den første til at hjælpe ham. Hans elfenbensben var knækket af, og der var kun en kort, skarp splint tilbage.
»Ja, ja, Starbuck, det er sødt at læne sig op ad nogen af og til, hvem det så er, der lænes op ad. Og jeg ville ønske, at gamle Ahab havde lænet sig oftere, end han har gjort.«
»Beslaget har ikke holdt, sir,« sagde tømreren, der nu kom hen til dem. »Jeg lagde godt arbejde i det ben.«
»Men ingen knogler brækket, sir, håber jeg,« sagde Stubb med ægte bekymring.

»Jo! Og splintret helt i stykker, Stubb! — kan du se det? — Men selv med en brækket knogle er gamle Ahab urørt. Og jeg regner ikke nogen levende knogle i mig for en tøddel mere mig end denne døde, der er tabt. Hverken hvid hval eller menneske eller djævel kan så meget som ridse gamle Ahab i hans eget, uopnåelige væsen. Kan noget lod nå gulvet dernede, kan noget mast skrabe taget deroppe? — Hallo, deroppe! Hvilken kant?«
»Lige for læ, sir.«
»Roret op, så, og sæt sejl igen, skibsvagter! Ned med resten af reservebådene og rig dem til. Mr. Starbuck, af sted, og mønstr bådenes besætninger.«
»Lad mig først hjælpe Dem hen til skansekledningen, sir.«
»Åh, åh, åh! Hvor splinten dog borer sig ind i mig nu! Forbandede skæbne! At den uovervindelige kaptajn i sjælen skal have så fej en styrmand!«
»Sir?«

»Min krop, mand, ikke dig. Giv mig noget at støtte mig til — der, den knuste lanse duer. Mønstr folkene. Jeg har sikkert ikke set ham endnu. Ved himlen, det kan ikke være! — mangler? — hurtigt! Kald dem alle sammen.«
Den gamle mands halvt udtalte tanke var sand. Da mandskabet var mønstret, var parseren der ikke.
»Parseren!« råbte Stubb — »han må være blevet fanget i — «
»Den sorte opkastning tage dig! — løb, alle sammen, oppe, nede, kahyt, mandskabsrum — find ham — ikke væk — ikke væk!«
Men de kom hurtigt tilbage til ham med den besked, at parseren ikke var til at finde nogen steder.
»Ja, sir,« sagde Stubb — »fanget i sammenfiltringen af Deres line — jeg syntes, jeg så ham blive trukket under.«

»Min line! Min line? Væk? — væk? Hvad betyder det lille ord? — Hvilken dødsklokke ringer i det, siden gamle Ahab ryster, som var han selve klokketårnet? Harpunen også! — kast alt skrammelet derovre over bord — kan I se den? — det smedede jern, folkens, den hvide hvals — nej, nej, nej — forbrændte tåbe! denne hånd kastede den! — den sidder i fisken! — Hallo, deroppe! Hold ham naglet fast — hurtigt! — alle mand til bådenes rigning — saml årerne — harpunerer! jernene, jernene! — hejs de øverste sejl højere — træk i alle skødene! — roret derovre! Hold kursen, hold kursen, om livet gælder det! Jeg skal omringe den umålelige klode ti gange, ja, og dykke lige gennem den, men jeg skal dræbe ham endnu!«

»Store Gud! Vis dig, bare for ét eneste øjeblik,« råbte Starbuck, »aldrig, aldrig får De ham fanget, gamle mand — i Jesu navn, ikke mere af dette; det er værre end djævelsk vanvid. To dages jagt, to gange slået i stykker, Deres eget ben revet væk under Dem endnu en gang, Deres onde skygge væk — alle gode engle omringer Dem med advarsler — hvad mere vil De have? — Skal vi blive ved med at jage denne morderiske fisk, til han har sænket den sidste mand? Skal vi lade ham trække os til bunden af havet? Skal vi lade ham slæbe os til underverdenen? Åh, åh — det er ugudelighed og blasfemi at jage ham længere!«

»Starbuck, på det seneste har jeg følt mig besynderligt draget mod dig, lige siden den time, da vi begge så — du ved hvad — i hinandens øjne. Men i denne sag med hvalen, så lad din ansigtsside være for mig som håndfladen her — en læbeløs, udtryksløs tomhed. Ahab er altid Ahab, mand. Hele denne handling er uforanderligt besluttet. Du og jeg øvede den en milliard år, før dette hav rullede. Tåbe! Jeg er Skæbnegudindernes løjtnant; jeg handler efter ordre. Sørg for, underordnede, at du adlyder min. — Stil jer rundt om mig, mænd. I ser en gammel mand fældet ned til stubben, lænet op ad en knust lanse, støttet på en ensom fod. Det er Ahab — hans krops del. Men Ahabs sjæl er en tusindben, der bevæger sig på hundrede ben. Jeg føler mig anstrengt, halvt strandet, som de tove, der slæber afmastede fregatter i storm, og sådan ser jeg måske også ud. Men før jeg knækker, vil I høre mig knage, og indtil I hører det, så ved, at Ahabs trosse endnu slæber hans mål. Tror I, mænd, på de ting, der kaldes varsler? Så le højt og råb da capo! For før de drukner, kommer drukknende ting op til overfladen to gange, og så op igen, for at synke for evigt. Sådan er det med Moby Dick — i to dage har han flydt — i morgen bliver den tredje. Ja, mænd, han kommer op en gang til — men kun for at sprøjte sit sidste! Føler I jer modige, mænd, modige?«
»Som frygtløs ild,« råbte Stubb.

»Og lige så mekanisk,« mumlede Ahab. Så, mens mændene gik frem mod stævnen, mumlede han videre: »De ting, der kaldes varsler! Og i går talte jeg på samme måde til Starbuck derovre om min ødelagte båd. Åh! hvor tappert jeg dog prøver at drive ud af andres hjerter, hvad der sidder så fast nittet i mit eget! — Parseren — parseren! — væk, væk? Og han skulle gå forud — men skulle dog ses igen, før jeg kunne omkomme — hvordan hænger det sammen? — Der er en gåde, der kunne forvirre alle advokater, bakket op af spøgelserne af hele rækken af dommere — den hakker i min hjerne som et høgenæb. Jeg — jeg skal nok løse den!«
Da tusmørket sænkede sig, var hvalen stadig i sigte for læ.

Så blev sejlene endnu en gang reduceret, og det meste forløb næsten som natten før. Bortset fra at lyden af hamre og brummen fra slibestenen kunne høres til næsten dagslys, mens mændene slæbte i lygtelys med den fuldstændige og omhyggelige rigning af reservebådene og slibningen af deres nye våben til næste dag. Imens lavede tømreren af den ødelagte kæl på Ahabs vragede båd et nyt ben til ham. Og som natten før stod Ahab foroverbøjet og stiv i sin lem, og hans skjulte heliotrop-blik — solsøgende som blomsten — var vendt tilbage på sit ur før tiden, indstillet mod øst for den tidligste sol.
